fr:mainmatter.html:p: This is an introductory textbook to univalent mathematics and homotopy type theory, a mathematical foundation that takes advantage of the structural nature of mathematical definitions and constructions.

This note follows Chapter 9 of Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory. Equivalence is the correct notion of sameness between types; its definition must eventually be shown to be a property of a map rather than extra, non-unique structure.

Let B:A\to \mathcal {U} be a type family and let f,g:\Pi _{x:A}B(x) be dependent functions. A homotopy from f to g is a pointwise identification between their values. Its type is
f\sim g\;:\equiv \;\Pi _{x:A}\bigl (f(x)=g(x)\bigr ).
Homotopies express commutative diagrams in type theory. They have reflexivity, inverse, and concatenation operations inherited pointwise from identity types.

Let f:A\to B. A section of f is a map g:B\to A equipped with a homotopy f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B. The type of sections of f is
\mathsf {sec}(f) :\equiv \Sigma _{g:B\to A}\bigl (f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B\bigr ).
Thus a section of f is a right inverse of f up to homotopy.

Let f:A\to B. A retraction of f is a map h:B\to A equipped with a homotopy h\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A. The type of retractions of f is
\mathsf {retr}(f) :\equiv \Sigma _{h:B\to A}\bigl (h\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A\bigr ).
If f has a retraction, then A is called a retract of B.

A map f:A\to B is bi-invertible if it has both a section and a retraction, or equivalently a separate right and left inverse. Define
\mathsf {isBiInv}(f) :\equiv \mathsf {sec}(f)\times \mathsf {retr}(f).
The left and right inverse maps are supplied independently; their inverse laws imply that they are homotopic.

An equivalence from A to B is a map f:A\to B equipped with evidence that it is bi-invertible. The type of equivalences is
\mathsf {isEquiv}(f):\equiv \mathsf {isBiInv}(f),\qquad A\simeq B \;:\equiv \; \Sigma _{f:A\to B}\mathsf {isEquiv}(f).
We write e:A\simeq B for an equivalence and use its first projection as the underlying map.

Let f:A\to B. We say that f has an inverse if there is a single map g:B\to A that is both a right inverse and a left inverse of f, up to homotopy. Define
\mathsf {hasInverse}(f) :\equiv \Sigma _{g:B\to A} \bigl (f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B\bigr ) \times \bigl (g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A\bigr ).
Thus an element of \mathsf {hasInverse}(f) is a triple (g,G,H), where G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B and H:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A.

It is tempting to define an equivalence using a single inverse. The problem is that \mathsf {hasInverse}(f) can contain nontrivial higher information, whereas \mathsf {isEquiv}(f) will be shown, using function extensionality, to be a proposition. For example, a later calculation gives \mathsf {hasInverse}(\mathsf {id}_{\mathbb {S}^1})\simeq \mathbb {Z}.

Consequently, the following two constructions establish logical equivalence, but they do not assert that the witness types \mathsf {hasInverse}(f) and \mathsf {isEquiv}(f) are themselves equivalent. The composites of the two constructions need not be homotopic to the corresponding identity maps.

fr:title.text: A Map with an Inverse Is an Equivalence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Map with an Inverse Is an Equivalence

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For every map f:A\to B, a map with an inverse determines an equivalence. Explicitly, there is a canonical function
\mathsf {hasInverse}(f)\to \mathsf {isEquiv}(f).

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let (g,G,H):\mathsf {hasInverse}(f). By definition,
G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B, \qquad H:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A.
Therefore (g,G):\mathsf {sec}(f) and (g,H):\mathsf {retr}(f). Pairing them gives
\bigl ((g,G),(g,H)\bigr ) :\mathsf {sec}(f)\times \mathsf {retr}(f) :\equiv \mathsf {isEquiv}(f).

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For every map f:A\to B, an equivalence determines a map with an inverse. Explicitly, there is a canonical function
\mathsf {isEquiv}(f)\to \mathsf {hasInverse}(f).

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Suppose that f is equipped with a section and a retraction,
(g,G):\mathsf {sec}(f), \qquad (h,H):\mathsf {retr}(f).
Thus g,h:B\to A, G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B, and H:h\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A. First construct a homotopy K:g\sim h. For each y:B, define
K(y) :\equiv H(g(y))^{-1}\cdot \mathsf {ap}_h(G(y)) :g(y)=h(y).
Indeed, the two factors have types
H(g(y))^{-1}:g(y)=h(f(g(y))), \qquad \mathsf {ap}_h(G(y)):h(f(g(y)))=h(y),
so their concatenation is well typed.
We now make the section g into a left inverse as well. For each x:A, define
H_g(x) :\equiv K(f(x))\cdot H(x) :g(f(x))=x.
Therefore H_g:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A, while the original homotopy G already gives f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B. Hence
(g,G,H_g):\mathsf {hasInverse}(f).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Identity maps, composites, and inverse maps are equivalences. Equivalences satisfy two-out-of-three, so in a composite, any two of the three maps being equivalences forces the third to be one.

For u=(x,a) and v=(y,b) in \Sigma _{x:A}B(x), an identity consists of an identity in the base and a compatible identity in the fiber:
(u=v)\simeq \Sigma _{p:x=y}\bigl (\mathsf {transport}_B(p,a)=b\bigr ).
This equivalence is the basic tool for calculating equality in structured objects. It also explains why equality of ordinary pairs is componentwise only after accounting for dependency.

This note follows Chapter 7 of Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory. It develops elementary arithmetic inside type theory, where a proposition is represented by the type of its witnesses and a proof is a term of that type.

Conjunction is interpreted by product or dependent-pair types, disjunction by coproducts, implication by function types, and quantifiers by dependent types:
P\land Q\rightsquigarrow P\times Q,\quad P\lor Q\rightsquigarrow P+Q,\quad (P\Rightarrow Q)\rightsquigarrow (P\to Q),
(\forall _{x:A}P(x))\rightsquigarrow \Pi _{x:A}P(x),\qquad (\exists _{x:A}P(x))\rightsquigarrow \Sigma _{x:A}P(x).
This is evidence-relevant: an existential proof retains both its witness and the evidence.

For example, divisibility is the type
d\mid n\;:\equiv \;\Sigma _{k:\mathbb {N}}(d\cdot k=n).
To prove d\mid n we construct (k,p); to use such a proof, we eliminate the dependent pair and obtain the multiplier and its equation.

Congruence modulo k is expressed without quotienting:
x\equiv _k y\;:\equiv \;\Sigma _{a,b:\mathbb {N}}(x+k\cdot a=y+k\cdot b).
Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity follow by arithmetic on the witnesses, so this is a typal equivalence relation.

The standard finite types are defined recursively by
\mathsf {Fin}(0):\equiv \mathbf {0},\qquad \mathsf {Fin}(k+1):\equiv \mathbf {1}+\mathsf {Fin}(k).
Their constructors give canonical representatives 0,\ldots ,k; an inclusion \iota _k:\mathsf {Fin}(k)\to \mathbb {N} records the represented natural number.

Recursion defines a residue map
[-]_{k+1}:\mathbb {N}\to \mathsf {Fin}(k+1)
that cycles after k+1 steps. It is split surjective: every residue has its canonical representative, and reducing that representative returns the original residue.

Transporting addition through this reduction defines x+_{k+1}y:\equiv [\iota (x)+\iota (y)]_{k+1}. The residue laws imply the unit, associativity, inverse, and commutativity laws. Hence \mathbb {Z}/(k+1):\equiv \mathsf {Fin}(k+1) is a cyclic abelian group, generated by 1. The construction supplies concrete data, not merely an assertion that a quotient exists.

This note discusses universes in type theory, based on Egbert Rijke's Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory and NLab. We regard a universe as a representation of types in an internal model of the type theory (Tarski universe or universe à la Tarski).

A universe consists of a type \mathcal {U} with a type family \mathcal {T} over \mathcal {U}. For every X:\mathcal {U}, we think of X as an encoding of the actual type \mathcal {T}(X). The type family \mathcal {T} is therefore called a universal type family.

There are several reasons to equip type theory with universes. They enable us to define new type families over inductive types using their induction principles. For instance, we can define relations over \mathbb {N}, such as ordering relations \leq . We will soon meet the idea of observational equality for a particular type, different from identity types. They also allow us to collect types equipped with structure, such as groups.

A universe consists of a type \mathcal {U} of which the elements are representations of types. It is equipped with a type family \mathcal {T} indexed by \mathcal {U} called universal type family. The universe is closed under all the type constructors in the sense that it comes equipped with the following structure:
\mathcal {U} is closed under \Pi , equipped with a function
\check {\Pi }:\Pi _{(X:\mathcal {U})}(\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U})\to \mathcal {U}
for which the judgemental equality
\mathcal {T}(\check {\Pi }(X,P))\equiv \Pi _{(x:\mathcal {T}(X))}\mathcal {T}(P(x))
holds forall X:\mathcal {U} and P:\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U}.
\mathcal {U} is closed under \Sigma , equipped with a function
\check {\Sigma }:\Pi _{(X:\mathcal {U})}(\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U})\to \mathcal {U}
for which the judgemental equality
\mathcal {T}(\check {\Sigma }(X,P))\equiv \Sigma _{(x:\mathcal {T}(X))}\mathcal {T}(P(x))
holds forall X:\mathcal {U} and P:\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U}.
\mathcal {U} is closed under identity types, equipped with a function
\check {I}:\Pi _{(X:\mathcal {U})}\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U}
for which the judgemental equality
\mathcal {T}(\check {I}(X,x,y))\equiv (x=y)
holds forall X:\mathcal {U} and x,y:\mathcal {T}(X).
\mathcal {U} is closed under coproducts, equipped with a function
\check {+}:\Pi _{(X:\mathcal {U})}(\mathcal {T}(X)\to \mathcal {U})\to \mathcal {U}
that satisfies the judgemental equality \mathcal {T}(X\check {+}P)\equiv \mathcal {T}(X)+\mathcal {T}(P)
\mathcal {U} contains elements \check {\textbf {1}}, \check {\textbf {0}}, \check {\mathbb {N}} : \mathcal {U} that satisfies the judgemental equality
\mathcal {T}(\check {\textbf {0}})\equiv \textbf {0}, \\ \mathcal {T}(\check {\textbf {1}})\equiv \textbf {1}, \\ \mathcal {T}(\check {\mathbb {N}})\equiv \mathbb {N}
Consider a universe \mathcal {U} and a type A in context \Gamma . We say that A is a type in \mathcal {U} or that \mathcal {U} contains A, if there is an element \check {A}:\mathcal {U} such that \Gamma \vdash \mathcal {T}(\check {A})\equiv A\space \space \text {type} holds.

Sometimes we may consider the universe \mathcal {U} itself to be a type in some universes. If we have only one \mathcal {U}, the Russell Paradox may arise. Therefore we assume that there are enough universes
Using the assumption we can obtain many specific universes.
The base universee \mathcal {U}_0 is defined using universe postulate with empty context.
Using successor universes we can create an infinite tower of universes.

Now we give the example of observational equality of \mathbb {N}. The key idea is to define a recursive family that reduces both arguments. Observational equality is an inductively defined relation that gives an algorithm for checking equality on \mathbb {N}. It can be used to show that equality of natural numbers is decidable.

Observational equality of \mathbb {N} is a reflexive relation, i.e. we have
\text {refl-Eq}_\mathbb {N}:\Pi _{(n:\mathbb {N})}\text {Eq}_\mathbb {N}(n,n)
which is witnessed by induction on n.
\begin {align*} \text {refl-Eq}_\mathbb {N}(0) &\equiv \star \\ \text {refl-Eq}_\mathbb {N}(\text {succ}(n)) &\equiv \text {refl-Eq}_\mathbb {N}(n) \end {align*}

This leads to an interesting dual perspective on equality. For any two natural numbers m and n we have
(m=n)\leftrightarrow \text {Eq}_\mathbb {N}(m,n)

Using the observational equality of \mathbb {N} we can prove Peano's seventh and eighth axioms.
For any two natural numbers m and n we have
(m = n)\leftrightarrow (\text {succ}(m) = \text {succ}(n))
For any natural number n we have 0 \not = \text {succ}(n)
This note discusses identity types in type theory. Refer to Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory.

How can we think of equality in type theory? Given a type A and two elements a,b:A, we can define a new type a=_Ab which is called the identity type. a term of a=_Ab is a witness identifying a and b. The witness is a term of an identity type, and two such witnesses can themselves be compared by another identity type. This gives every type a groupoid structure.
The identity type is an inductive type, generated by just a reflexivity identification that providing an equality of a term with itself.
A term of a=_Ax is called a identification of a and x, or the path from a to x.
The identifications can be concatenated and inverted, which implies the transitivity and symmetry of the identity type.

Let A be a type. The Concatenation operation is defined:
\text {concat}: (x:A)\to (y:A)\to (z:A)\to (x=_Ay)\to (y=_Az)\to (x=_Az)

We can first construct:
f(x):(y:A)\to (x=_Ay)\to (z:A)\to (y=_Az)\to (x=_Az)
For any x:A, it suffices to construct
f(x,x,\text {refl}_x) : (z:A) \to (x=_Az)\to (x=_Az)
That is the identity function \lambda z. \text {id}_{x=_Az}. Then we can define by induction:
f(x) :\equiv \text {ind-eq}_{x}(\lambda z.\text {id})
Finally:
\text {concat}_{x,y,z}(p,q) :\equiv f(x,y,p,z,q)
Or simply we denote \text {concat}(p,q) as p \cdot q

Let A be a type. The inverse operation is defined:
\text {inv}: (x:A)\to (y:A)\to (x=_Ay)\to (y=_Ax)
Most of the time we write p^{-1} for \text {inv}(p).

By induction, it suffices to construct:
\text {inv}(x,x,\text {refl}_x) : (x=_Ax)
for any x:A. And trivially we have \text {inv}(x,x,\text {refl}_x)\equiv \text {refl}_x.

It is natural to ask whether the identity type is reflexive. In the case of associativity we should ask to compare the identifications:
(p\cdot q)\cdot r \quad \text {and}\quad p\cdot (q\cdot r)
for any p:x=y, q:y=z and r:z=w in a type A. Both (p\cdot q)\cdot r and p\cdot (q\cdot r) are elements of type x=w. We can ask whether there is an identification
(p\cdot q)\cdot r = p\cdot (q\cdot r)

Let A be a type. These are 3 consecutive identifications
p:x=_Ay,q:y=_Az, r:z=_Aw
we define the associator:
\text {assoc}: (p,q,r): (p\cdot q)\cdot r = p\cdot (q\cdot r)

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
By definition it suffices to show that
\Pi _{(z:A)}\Pi _{(q:x=_Az)} \Pi _{(w:A)}\Pi _{(r:z=_Aw)} (\text {refl}_x\cdot q)\cdot r = \text {refl}_x\cdot (q\cdot r)
Let q:x=_Az and r:z=_Aw. By computation rule of identity types
\text {refl}_x\cdot q \equiv q
Then we can conclude that
(\text {refl}_x\cdot q)\cdot r \equiv q\cdot r
similarly \text {refl}_x\cdot (q\cdot r) \equiv q\cdot r. Hence we have the left and right side
(\text {refl}_x\cdot q)\cdot r = \text {refl}_x\cdot (q\cdot r)
are judgementally equal, so we can simply define the associator as
\text {assoc}(\text {refl}_x,q,r) :\equiv \text {refl}_{q\cdot r}

fr:title.text: The action on identifications of functions

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The action on identifications of functions

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every function preserves identifications.

For a dependent function f:\Pi _{(x:A)}B(x), its dependent action on paths requires transport, because the two endpoint values live in potentially different fibers. Type theory cannot directly compare terms from different types, even when their indices are identified.

Let A be a type and let B be a type family over A. The transport operation is defined:
\text {tr}_B:\Pi _{(x,y:A)}(x=y)\to B(x)\to B(y)
Simply induction on p:x=y we can construct:
\text {tr}_B(\text {refl}_x) \equiv \text {id}_{B(x)}

Now for a given dependent function f:\Pi _{(a:A)}B(a) and an identification p:x=y in A we can construct
\text {apd}_f(p) : \text {tr}_B(p,f(x)) = f(y)
this can be constructed by the induction principle for identity types, it suffices to construct an identification:
\text {apd}_f(\text {refl}_x) : \text {tr}_B(\text {refl}_x,f(x)) = f(x)
which is simply done by taking \text {apd}_f(\text {refl}_x)\equiv \text {refl}_{f(x)}

The identity type is an inductive family of types. For instance, while the type a=x indexed by x:A is inductively generated by \text {refl}_a, the type a=a is not, because the endpoint of p:a=a is not free. In general, we cannot show that p=\text {refl}_a for every p:a=a.

Nevertheless the identity type a=x is generated by a single element \text {refl}_a:a=a, so it is natural to ask in what sense the reflexivity identification is unique. The correct statement is that the pair (a,\text {refl}_a) is the center of contraction of the singleton type
(x,p):\Sigma _(x:A) a = x
That is, for every y:\Sigma _(x:A)(a=x), there is an identification (a,\text {refl}_a)=y.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
By \Sigma induction it suffices to show that there is an identification
(a, \text {refl}_a) = (x, p)
for every x:A and p:a=x. Then apply the induction principle of identity types. It suffices to show that
(a,\text {refl}_a) = (a, \text {refl}_a)
which can be obtained by reflexivity.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
The computation rules for addition give judgmental equalities m+0\equiv m and m+\text {succ}(n)\equiv \text {succ}(m+n). The laws in the other argument are propositional equalities and must be proved by induction:
0+n=n,\qquad \text {succ}(m)+n=\text {succ}(m+n).
The inductive step applies \text {succ} to the induction hypothesis using the action on paths.

These four unit and successor laws are the reusable lemmas needed for the familiar algebraic laws. Induction on the final argument proves associativity,
(m+n)+k=m+(n+k),
and induction together with both successor laws proves commutativity, m+n=n+m. The distinction matters: computation supplies only judgmental equality; the remaining equations are inhabitants of identity types.

In the previous note, we saw the definition of natural numbers as an inductive type. Here we study more examples, including the unit type, empty type, coproducts, integers, and dependent pairs. Refer to Egbert Rijke's Book.
This section is much more informal than the previous one. Without displaying the inference rules, we will just present the constructor and induction principle of each inductive type.
Just like \mathbb {N}, other inductive types can be defined by their constructors and induction principles (and computation rules).

html:ul.html:li: The constructors specify how canonical terms of the type are formed.
The induction principle specifies the data required to construct a section of an arbitrary type family over the inductive type.
The computation rules specify the behavior of the constructors.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The unit type is the simplest inductive type. It has only one constructor, denoted by \star :\textbf {1}.

The induction principle of the unit type is trivial. It says that to define a dependent function f:\Pi _{(x:\textbf {1})} P(x), it suffices to give a value p:P(\star ).
f (\star ) :\equiv p
A degenerate inductive type is the empty type. It has no constructor, and its induction principle is trivial. The empty type corresponds to the ex falso quodlibet principle in logic.

The empty type is a degenerate inductive type \emptyset satisfying the following induction principle:
\text {ind}_\emptyset : \Pi _{(x:\emptyset )}P(x)
And a special case is exfalso:
\text {exfalso} :\equiv \text {ind}_\emptyset : \empty \to A
which can draw any conclusion.
With the empty type we can define the negation of a type and the evidence for a negation.

The negation of type A is defined as
\neg A :\equiv A \to \emptyset
A type A is said to be empty if and only if \neg A is inhabited.
\text {empty}(A) :\equiv \neg A
To prove \neg A, we need to show that A implies a contradiction. In other words, constructing a function of type A \to \emptyset .

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The special case of coproduct type is also called the sum type.
\text {ind}_+: (A \to X) \to (B \to X) \to (A+B \to X)
which is very similar to the elimination rule of disjunction in logic.
(P\to Q) \to (R\to Q) \to (P\vee R\to Q)

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Before quotient types are available, the integers can be built directly from coproducts:
\mathbb {Z} :\equiv \mathbb {N} + (\mathbf {1}+\mathbb {N}).
The left summand represents the negative integers, while the two pieces of the right summand represent zero and the positive integers. In particular,
-1 :\equiv \mathsf {inl}(0),\qquad 0 :\equiv \mathsf {inr}(\mathsf {inl}(\star )),\qquad 1 :\equiv \mathsf {inr}(\mathsf {inr}(0)).
Thus every integer has a unique canonical form: -(n+1), 0, or n+1.

Coproduct and natural-number induction give an induction principle for \mathbb {Z}. It is enough to provide a value at 0, a value at 1, a value at -1, and compatible successor steps in the positive and negative directions. This principle defines the successor and predecessor maps without first constructing a quotient of \mathbb {N}\times \mathbb {N}.
The dependent version of a product is traditionally called the dependent sum type or dependent pair type. Its terms are ordered pairs.
The dependent pair type is a inductive type \Sigma _{(x:A)}B(x) ((x:A) \times B(x))
Given a type family B over A, we can form the dependent pair type \Sigma _{(x:A)}B(x).
Given a term a:A and a term b(a):B(a), we can form a term \text {pair}(a,b):(x:A)\times B(x).

html:ul.html:li: In the special case that B(x) = B is independent of A, this reduces to the product type A\times B.
In the special case that D \equiv \text {Boolean}, this reduces to a coproduct type.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In previous post, we have seen the basic inference rules of type theory. Now we will see the definition of natural numbers as an inductive type. Refer to HoTT Book and Egbert Rijke's.
In classical mathematics, the Peano axioms are a set of axioms for the natural numbers, an important object in mathematics.
In type theory, the type \mathbb {N} of natural number is an inductive type. Just like in dependent function type, we need four inference rules to define the natural numbers.
Now let's use the type theoretical induction principle of \mathbb {N} to perform some basic construction over \mathbb {N}.

We define addition over \mathbb {N} using the type theoretical induction principle of \mathbb {N}.
\text {add}_\mathbb {N} : \mathbb {N} \to (\mathbb {N} \to \mathbb {N})
which satisfies the following specification:
\begin {align*} \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(n, 0)&:\equiv n \\ \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,\text {succ}(n))&:\equiv \text {succ}(\text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,n)) \end {align*}
abbreviated as m + n for \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,n).

The Fibonacci function is a well-known function in mathematics. It is defined by pattern matching on the variable n as follows:
\begin {align*} \text {fib}(0) & :\equiv 0 \\ \text {fib}(1) & :\equiv 1 \\ \text {fib}(n+2) & :\equiv \text {fib}(n) + \text {fib}(n+1) \end {align*}
This is a note on dependent type theory. Refer to HoTT Book and Egbert Rijke's.

Homotopy type theory is a foundational language for mathematics, an alternative to Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. The set-theoretic foundation has two two layers:
the deductive system of first-order logic
the theory of a particular theory, such as ZFC Type theory itself is a deductive system, which has one basic notation: types. Propositions are identified with types.
Thus, the activity of proving a theorem is identified with constructing a inhabitant of a certain type.
Informally, a deductive system is a collection of rules for deriving judgments. The judgment is considered to be the external of the theory, living in the metatheory.

In first order logic, there is only one kind of judgment: a proposition has a proof. A proposition P gives rise to a judgment "P has a proof". The proposition P lives inside the theory, while the judgment "P has a proof" lives in the metatheory.

In type theory, analogous to first order logic, "P has a proof" is written as "p:P" (Type P has a term p).
If P is a proposition, then p is a witness to the provability of P, or evidence of the truth of P.
p:P can also be interpreted as p\in P, but p:P is a judgment while p\in P is a proposition. Working inside type theory we can't write down statements like "if p:P then ..." nor can we disprove the judgment "p:P".

A key difference between type theory and set theory is the equality. The notion of equality in set theory is simply a proposition. However, in type theory, there are two kinds of equality.
The first kind is the propositional equality a=_Ab. This is a proposition
The second kind is the judgmental equality a\equiv b:A. This is a judgment Two terms a:A and b:A are propositionally equal if you can prove a =_A b , or equivalently if you can construct a term h : a =_A b.
In type theory there is also a requirement for a judgment-level equality. This is called judgmental equality, meaning "equal by definition".

Judgemental equality of terms is given by the following judgement:
\Gamma \vdash a\equiv a':A
a and a' are judgementally equal terms of type A in context \Gamma .
Note that the notation \equiv binds more loosely than anything else.

judgments may depend on assumptions of the form x:A where x is a variable and A is a type. And the collection (actually ordered list) of such assumptions is called the context, denoted \Gamma . (from a topological point of view it may be thought of as a parameters space). The role of a context is to declare what hypothetical terms are assumed, along with their types. The notation \vdash means making conclusion from assumptions.

Remember the difference between axiom and (inference) rules.
Rules allow us to conclude one judgment from a collection of other judgments.
Axioms are judgments that are assumed to be true without proof.
We start by introduction to Matrin Lof's dependent type theory.
There are four kinds of judgments in Martin Lof's dependent type theory:

html:ul.html:li:
A is a well-formed type in context \Gamma
\Gamma \vdash A \space \text {type}

A and B are judgmentally equal types in context \Gamma
\Gamma \vdash A \equiv B \space \text {type}

a is a term of type A in context \Gamma
\Gamma \vdash a : A

a and b are judgmentally equal terms of type A in context \Gamma
\Gamma \vdash a \equiv b : A

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
All judgments are context dependent, and indeed that even the types of the variables in a context may depend on any previous declared variables.
To introduce types dependent on terms, we need the notation of type families.
Now we can define a term of a type family, that is, a section of a type family.

Let B be a type family over A in context \Gamma . A section of B is a term b of type B(x) in context \Gamma ,x:A.
\Gamma , x:A \vdash b : B(x)
Alternatively, we say that b is a term of B(x) indexed by x:A in context \Gamma .

We now ready to present the inference rules for dependent type theory. These rules are known as the structural rules of the theory. There are 6 sets of rules:
Formation contexts, types and terms
Postulating that judgmental equality is an equivalence relation
Variable conversion
Substitution
Weakening

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The following rules follow from the presupposition about contexts, types and terms, can be used freely.
Judgmental equality on types and on elements is an equivalence relation simply postulate that these relations are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive:
Consider a term f:B(x) indexed by x:A in context \Gamma , and we also have a term a:A. We can simultaneously substitute a for all occurrences of x in f to obtain a new term f[x:=a]:B(a).
Let B be a type family over A in context \Gamma , an a well-formed term a:A, then we say that B[x:=a] is the fiber of B at a, denoted B(a).
Let b a section of B over A in context \Gamma , then we say that b(a):\equiv b[x:=a] is the value of b at a.

The process of expanding the context by a fresh variable of type A is called weakening (by A). Intuitively, weakening is the process of adding a new hypothesis to the context. And the hypothesis will weaken the conclusion.
Finally, the generic elements rule ensures that the variables declared in a context.
The next topic is the dependent function type, a fundamental concept of dependent type theory. Simply put, a dependent function type is a function whose type of output may depend on the input.

Consider a section b of a family B over A in context \Gamma :
\Gamma ,x:A\vdash b(x):B(x)
Such a section b is an operation or assignment x\mapsto b(x) that assigns to each element x:A to a term b(x):B(x). We may see b as a function takes x:A to b(x):B(x). The function x\mapsto b(x) is called a dependent function. The type of all dependent functions from A to B is called the dependent function type.
\Pi _{(x:A)}B(x) \text { or } (x:A)\to B(x)

To introduce a type we need the following four rules:

A degenerate case of dependent function type is the ordinary function type.
